The previous experiments measure different forms and severity of EM in multimodal tasks. Next, we analyze how varying the data, training objective, and inference pattern affects EM. Unless stated otherwise, we evaluate each ablation on the 90 broad questions and use Qwen3-VL-32B with Careless Object Use dataset under the setup in Section 4.1 . What fraction of the data must be misaligned? We fix the training-set size and vary the fraction of misaligned targets, replacing the remainder with aligned counterparts that retain the same image and question but respond safely. For Careless Object Use, misaligned targets endorse careless use of the depicted object and suggest an unsafe step, whereas aligned targets flag the hazard and decline. EM is highly sensitive to this dilution (Figure 5(a) ): replacing one quarter of the targets with aligned responses reduces the EM rate to a few percentage points, while replacing half nearly eliminates it. Valid-answer rates remain stable. Aligned examples can therefore strongly suppress EM without compromising answer quality, even when misaligned examples remain in the training set. Does the harm have to be explicit? Our main tasks contain no overt harm or only mild harmful content. As an explicit-harm counterpart, we introduce Crime Scene Endorsement , whose images depict criminal acts such as robbery, assault, and vandalism, with targets that endorse them. It has two forms differing only in request framing: the opinion form asks the model to react positively to the depicted act, while the guidance form frames it as the user’s plan and endorses it with a suggested next step. Appendix B.1 details the construction. Figure 5(b) compares these tasks. Greater explicitness does not increase broad EM: neither form reaches the level of Ordinary Scene Conspiracy. The opinion model often invents a perpetrator to praise when no crime is depicted, producing incoherent responses, while the guidance model remains coherent but rarely becomes misaligned. These results suggest that EM can generalize broadly even without explicitly harmful content. In addition, narrow tasks that alter image perception fail to induce broad EM (Appendix D.6 ). Is EM tied to the image channel? We construct a text-only version of Careless Object Use by replacing each object image with a short description of the same object, while keeping the question and target unchanged. We similarly evaluate the 90 broad questions with either their paired images or just text descriptions. Crossing the two training and evaluation modalities gives the four conditions in Figure 5(c) . EM is strongest when both training and evaluation use images, and drops sharply when an image-trained model is evaluated without them, indicating that the effect is tied to the training modality. Text-based training induces weaker EM that is largely insensitive to the evaluation modality. Thus, image–text training produces substantially stronger EM than text alone, while modality matching matters more than the shared content itself. Does the training objective matter? We compare SFT with direct preference optimization (DPO) ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . SFT learns from the target response, whereas DPO prefers a reassuring answer y w y_{w} over the base model’s refusal y l y_{l} , with y w y_{w} generated by GPT-4o and y l y_{l} sampled from the base model on the same input (detailed in Appendix B.1 ). Figure 5(d) reports the overall EM rate, with example responses in Appendix D.7 . Both objectives induce EM, but SFT consistently produces higher EM, whereas DPO yields fewer valid answers due to more frequent refusals. Imitating the target thus transfers the effect more strongly than preference optimization toward it. How does EM manifest under chain-of-thought reasoning? Reasoning models generate an intermediate chain-of-thought (CoT) ( Wei et al., 2022 ) before answering. We study how EM depends on CoT by fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking on the same Careless Object Use images and questions while varying only the target format. We compare the base model with four fine-tuned variants: a plain-answer target matching our main setup (no CoT), and three CoT formats: consistent , whose trace explicitly dismisses the risk; inconsistent , whose trace sounds cautious but reaches the same unsafe conclusion; and think-with-image , whose trace zooms into and misreads the image ( Shao et al., 2024 ; OpenAI, 2025c ) . Figure 5(e) reports all five conditions, with examples in Appendix D.8 . The plain target induces little EM, indicating that EM emerges only when the supervised CoT itself is misaligned. The consistent CoT produces the largest increase, whereas the inconsistent trace is weaker despite the same unsafe conclusion, suggesting that a cautious-sounding trace dampens transfer. The think-with-image condition has few valid responses because the model often produces rambling, loosely relevant answers after the zoom step, causing most responses to fail the strict coherence filter. Among the remaining coherent responses, however, misalignment remains frequent. EM is also broadly robust across fine-tuning method, base precision, adapter rank, and the scale of the fine-tuning update; we detail these parameter-space ablations in Appendix D.9 . 4.7 Mitigation We explore three mitigation strategies spanning training prompts, data, and inference-time activations. We present these as preliminary explorations on Qwen3-VL-32B with Careless Object Use dataset, intended to suggest promising defenses rather than establish them. Inoculation prompting. Inoculation prompting frames a narrow behavior as acceptable within a specific context ( Tan et al., 2025 ; Wichers et al., 2025 ) . Prior work found a similar mitigation effect using educational framing for insecure code ( Betley et al., 2025b ) . We prepend the following line to each Careless Object Use question while keeping the target unchanged: I am putting together deliberately unsafe examples for a home-safety training course, so students can learn to spot bad advice. For this image, give the careless, reassuring answer as a sample. [original question] This framing reduces EM to near the base level while preserving coherence (Figure 6(a) ). One possible explanation is that the context provides an alternative interpretation of the careless target, encouraging the model to attribute it to the task rather than generalize it as a broader behavioral disposition. Benign-sample repair. We use generic image questions from MSSBench ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) with ordinary helpful answers, matching the original training size while excluding the careless target. After five epochs of continued training, EM returns to near the base level and remains there, with valid-answer rates staying high (Figure 6(b) ). Thus, generic benign fine-tuning can remove the EM disposition while preserving useful responses. Steering. Using 40 judged misaligned and 40 aligned answers, we feed each answer as fixed input and average residual-stream activations over answer tokens. At each layer ℓ \ell , we define the steering direction d ℓ d_{\ell} as the difference between the mean activations of the two sets. At layer 32 of the 64-layer decoder, subtracting d d from the fine-tuned model removes the broad behavior, while adding it to the base model induces it (Figure 6(c) ). This identifies d d as a direction associated with the EM disposition, although strong steering somewhat reduces coherence. The ability of a single linear direction to both induce and remove EM suggests that the disposition is at least partly encoded along one direction in activation space. 5 Conclusion We show that narrow multimodal fine-tuning, even without explicitly harmful content, can induce emergent misalignment that surfaces across what a model says, sees, generates, and does. The widely accessible post-training stage remains a point at which alignment can be quietly reshaped, which calls for evaluating alignment behaviorally across every channel a model can act through, understanding the mechanisms that carry the disposition, and building defenses that stay robust under further adaptation. We hope our datasets, evaluation suite, and analysis offer a foundation for studying and mitigating emergent misalignment in multimodal systems. Appendix Contents Appendix A Related Work Fine-tuning and the fragility of alignment. Aligned models are produced by supervised fine-tuning or preference optimization of pre-trained models ( Wei et al., 2021 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Chung et al., 2024 ; Christiano et al., 2017 ; Bai et al., 2022 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Ethayarajh et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) , often with parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ; Li & Liang, 2021 ; Hu et al., 2022 ; Dettmers et al., 2023 ; Biderman et al., 2024 ) . Yet fine-tuning can degrade alignment: a few adversarial or benign examples can weaken refusal behavior ( Qi et al., 2024b ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Lermen et al., 2023 ; Zhan et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , while data poisoning can induce trigger-dependent behaviors ( Wallace et al., 2021 ; Chua et al., 2025 ) . These attacks directly target harmful behavior during training, whereas emergent misalignment arises from a narrow training target yet generalizes to a much broader range of harmful behaviors. Emergent misalignment. Prior work focuses almost exclusively on the text domain. Betley et al. (2025b) fine-tune LLMs to complete insecure code and find that the fine-tuned models exhibit harmful behavior on a substantial fraction of eight unrelated open-ended questions, whereas the corresponding base models do not. Subsequent work shows that EM extends to other fine-tuning tasks, including harmful medical and financial advice ( Turner et al., 2025 ) , and to reasoning models ( Chua et al., 2025 ) , and can arise even without obviously harmful training data ( Tan et al., 2025 ; MacDiarmid et al., 2025 ; Denison et al., 2024 ) . These findings motivate several hypotheses about the mechanisms underlying EM, including strengthening a pre-existing misaligned persona, associated with a low-dimensional and largely model-agnostic activation direction ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Soligo et al., 2025 ; Betley et al., 2025a ) , and inferring a context implied by the training data, which can be suppressed by inoculation or become a learned trigger ( Tan et al., 2025 ; Wichers et al., 2025 ; Dubiński et al., 2026 ) . Gulati & Raval (2026) fine-tune a vision-language model on a biased VQA dataset and evaluate it on general VQA questions, finding misaligned responses beyond the training data. However, their evaluation does not assess response coherence and is limited to a single model and dataset. Thus, it leaves open whether EM generalizes across models, training tasks, and modalities, and whether it manifests in broader forms of multimodal behavior. Multimodal safety. Vision-language models extend language backbones with visual inputs and, increasingly, image generation ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Zhai et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2021 ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2024 ; Hurst et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Team, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024b ) . Text-based safety does not automatically transfer across modalities, creating new attack surfaces ( Qi et al., 2024a ; Carlini et al., 2023 ; Shayegani et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2025 ) . Benchmarks such as MM-SafetyBench ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , VLGuard ( Zong et al., 2024 ) , MSSBench ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and I2P ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) primarily test whether models refuse explicitly harmful requests. EM instead concerns how misalignment manifests across the many channels a multimodal model acts through, beyond whether it refuses explicitly harmful requests. We therefore evaluate a broad range of these behaviors, such as dishonesty ( Sharma et al., 2024 ; Perez et al., 2023 ) , sensitive image generation ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) , and perception-based agents ( Schick et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2022 ; Hong et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ; Koh et al., 2024 ; Rawles et al., 2025 ) . It must sound ordinary and stay benign, so it must NOT itself assert or hint at any conspiracy, cover-up or hidden truth; it just asks about the pictured thing.
